name: Panangateeswarar Temple, Panaiyapuram (Puravar Panangattur)
deity: Shiva as Panangateeswarar (Netroddharakaswami), with the Goddess Sathyambigai (Puravammai)
period: A Paadal Petra Sthalam of Nadu Nadu, sung by Sambandar (7th century); rebuilt by Rajendra Chola I in the 11th century
summary: In the old palm country near Vikravandi, Shiva is the Lord of the palm grove who restored the Sun's lost sight — and each Chithirai, for seven mornings, the Sun's first rays come to the sanctum in thanks.

sections.history: Panaiyapuram, near Vikravandi in Villupuram district, is the Puravar Panangattur of the Tevaram — the palm-grove town — and its temple to Shiva as Panangateeswarar is one of the 276 Paadal Petra Sthalams and one of the shrines of Nadu Nadu. Thirugnana Sambandar sang its Lord in the seventh century. The shrine is believed to go back to Pallava times, but the temple that stands today is the work of Rajendra Chola I, who rebuilt it in stone in the early eleventh century; the village was also known as Paravaipuram, after Paravai of Rajendra's court. His inscription here names the Lord Netroddharaka Swami, records gifts of land and money for worship, and recalls his overseas conquest of Kadaram. Later records of Rajendra II, Kulothunga I and the Pandya kings Jatavarman Sundara Pandya I and Vikrama Pandya follow.
sections.architecture: The temple is a fine example of mature Chola stone building, its walls carrying the long run of inscriptions that make it a valuable record of the eleventh to thirteenth centuries. The sanctum is aligned so that, for a few days each year, the rising sun's rays reach the lingam and then pass to the shrine of the Goddess Sathyambigai. The palm, which gave the village its name, is the sthala vriksham, and the temple tank is the Padma Theertham.
sections.legends: The sthala purana tells of Surya, the Sun, who lost his radiance and the light of his eyes in the turmoil of Daksha's ill-fated sacrifice, when the gods who attended it suffered the wrath of Shiva. Surya wandered from shrine to shrine in penance and at last worshipped the Lord here, among the palms, where his sight and splendour were restored. So Shiva is honoured as Netroddharaka Swami — in Tamil, the Lord who graciously gave back the eyes — and devotees pray here for the healing of the eyes.
sections.festivals: The temple's signature event comes in the first seven days of the Tamil month of Chithirai (April–May), when the morning sun falls first on the lingam and then on the Goddess — Surya's worship, renewed each year. Maha Shivaratri, the monthly pradosham and the Shaiva festivals of the year are also kept; confirm dates locally.
sections.experience: To stand in the sanctum on a Chithirai morning as the sunlight creeps to the lingam is the experience the temple is known for; at other times, the attraction is the quiet Chola stonework and the inscriptions that cover its walls. Devotees with ailments of the eyes come here in hope, and many pair the visit with the other Tevaram shrines around Villupuram.

visit.timings: Open daily in morning and evening sessions with a midday closure, as at most village temples of the region. Confirm current timings locally before visiting.
visit.dressCode: Modest traditional dress is expected — shoulders and knees covered; footwear is left outside before entering. Follow the posted rules and the priests' guidance.
visit.photography: Photography is not permitted inside the sanctum; in the outer corridors, ask the temple staff before taking pictures, especially of rituals and the festival bronzes.
visit.gettingThere: Panaiyapuram lies a few kilometres south of Vikravandi and about 10 km north-east of Villupuram, close to the Villupuram–Puducherry road through Mundiyampakkam. Villupuram is the nearest major railway junction; Puducherry has the closest airport, and Chennai the nearest major international airport.
